lead: A hole in a tank, a short tube pushed into that hole, a V-shaped cut in a channel wall: all three ask the same question, how much flows out? Bernoulli gives the ideal answer from the head alone. The real answer differs only by a coefficient, and that coefficient splits into a contraction part and a velocity part. This is how canals, irrigation outlets and rooftop tanks are gauged, and how a notch of known shape becomes a cheap flow meter.
prereq: You need Bernoulli's equation from 3.3 and the continuity equation from Unit 2, Fluid Kinematics.

sections.h3: The orifice and its three coefficients

blocks.text: An orifice is a hole in the wall or bottom of a tank. A sharp-edged orifice is cut in a thin plate, so the jet touches the plate only along a line. Put point 1 on the free surface and point 2 in the jet just outside the hole. Both are at atmospheric pressure, and the tank is large, so the surface velocity is nearly zero. Bernoulli then gives the ideal jet speed.

blocks.where: V is the ideal jet speed in m/s, g = 9.81 m/s² is the gravitational acceleration, and H is the head of water above the centre of the orifice in m.

blocks.text: The real jet is slower because of friction, and thinner than the hole. Streamlines keep converging for a short distance outside the hole, so the jet is narrowest a little downstream. That section is the vena contracta. Cc = a<sub>c</sub>/a is the coefficient of contraction, jet area over hole area a, about 0.62 for a sharp edge. Cv = V<sub>actual</sub>/V is the coefficient of velocity, about 0.98. Their product is the coefficient of discharge, Cd = Cc Cv, about 0.62.

blocks.where: Q is the discharge in m³/s, a is the area of the hole in m², Cd = Cc Cv ≈ 0.62, and H is the head above the centre of the hole in m.

blocks.text: A small orifice has H more than about five hole diameters, so the head is nearly the same at the top and bottom of the hole. A large orifice does not, and its discharge is integrated over the height: Q = (2/3) Cd b √(2g) (H<sub>2</sub><sup>3/2</sup> − H<sub>1</sub><sup>3/2</sup>), where b is the width of the hole and H<sub>1</sub>, H<sub>2</sub> are the depths from the surface to the top and bottom edges.

sections.h3: Mouthpieces: a short tube on the same hole

blocks.text: A mouthpiece is a short tube, two or three diameters long, fixed to the hole. An external mouthpiece projects outside the tank. An internal or re-entrant mouthpiece projects inside.

The external cylindrical mouthpiece has Cd ≈ 0.82, well above the 0.62 of the bare hole. The vena contracta forms inside the tube, and the space between it and the outlet runs below atmospheric pressure. That suction pulls extra water through, provided the tube runs full. If the pressure at the vena contracta falls to vapour pressure, air enters and the coefficient drops back to about 0.62.

The Borda mouthpiece is an internal tube whose jet does not touch the tube walls, so there is no suction behind the jet and Cd ≈ 0.5. A converging mouthpiece recovers pressure along its length and gives a discharge coefficient much closer to 1.

sections.h3: Notches and weirs: integrating over the depth

blocks.text: A notch is a cut in the side of a tank or channel, with its top edge open to the air. A weir is a crest built across an open channel with water flowing over it. A sharp-crested weir is a thin plate with a sharp upstream edge, and the same theory covers it.

Take a rectangular notch of crest length L with head H over the crest. A horizontal strip at depth h below the surface, of thickness dh, passes water at speed √(2gh) through area L dh, so dQ = Cd L √(2gh) dh. Integrating h from 0 to H gives the working formula.

blocks.where: Q is the discharge in m³/s, Cd ≈ 0.6 for a sharp-crested weir, L is the crest length in m, g = 9.81 m/s², and H is the head over the crest in m.

blocks.text: A triangular or V-notch of full angle θ has strip width 2(H − h) tan(θ/2) at depth h. The same integration now runs into a 5/2 power.

blocks.where: θ is the full angle of the notch, H is the head over the vertex in m, and the other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: The higher power suits a V-notch to small flows, because the head does not become too tiny to read. A rectangular weir suits large flows.

End contraction: if the crest is shorter than the channel, the jet draws in at each end and the effective length becomes L − 0.1nH, where n counts the contracting ends, 0 for a suppressed weir spanning the full width and 2 for a crest clear of both sides. Velocity of approach: if the approach velocity in the channel is V<sub>a</sub>, its head h<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>a</sub>²/2g adds to H, so replace H by H + h<sub>a</sub>. The Francis formula folds the coefficient into one number for a suppressed rectangular weir: Q = 1.84 L H<sup>3/2</sup> in SI units, with Q in m³/s, L in m and H in m; with approach velocity the head term becomes (H + h<sub>a</sub>)<sup>3/2</sup> − h<sub>a</sub><sup>3/2</sup>. Trapezoidal and Cipolletti weirs have sloped sides that keep the coefficient steady as the head changes.

figure.caption: Four flow openings and the single number each one needs. The two holes are holes under pressure, scaled by a discharge coefficient; the two crests are open to the air, so their discharge follows a power of the head.

spec.aria: A tree of flow openings: an orifice and a mouthpiece, which are holes with discharge coefficients, and a notch and a weir, which are open crests whose discharge follows a power of the head.

examples.question: A rectangular sharp-crested weir spans the full width of a channel, so there are no end contractions. The crest length is 3 m and the head over the crest is 0.40 m. Take Cd = 0.62 and neglect the velocity of approach. (a) Find the discharge. (b) The same 3 m crest is now installed so that one end is clear of the side wall (one end contraction); the crest length is still 3 m. Find the new discharge at the same head.
steps: (b) One end contraction: L<sub>eff</sub> = L − 0.1nH = 3 − 0.1 × 1 × 0.40 = 3 − 0.04 = 2.96 m.
examples.answer: (a) The discharge is 1.389 m³/s, about 1.39 m³/s. (b) With one end contraction it falls to 1.371 m³/s, about 1.3 % less.
examples.check:
import math
Cd = 0.62
L = 3.0
H = 0.40
g = 9.81
Q = (2/3) * Cd * L * math.sqrt(2*g) * H**1.5
print(round(Q, 3))
Leff = L - 0.1 * 1 * H
Q2 = (2/3) * Cd * Leff * math.sqrt(2*g) * H**1.5
print(round(Q2, 3))

traps: Head read in the wrong place. For a weir, read H three to four H upstream of the crest, where the surface is still flat. For an orifice, read H to the centre of the hole.
Forgetting the end contraction L − 0.1nH, or using n = 2 for a suppressed weir that touches both walls. A suppressed weir has n = 0.
Borrowing a coefficient across devices. Orifice Cd ≈ 0.62, external mouthpiece ≈ 0.82, sharp-crested weir ≈ 0.6. Each belongs to its own device and edge condition.

Mixing Cc and Cd. Cd = Cc × Cv is smaller than either one. Writing it upside down as Cd = Cv / Cc gives 0.98 / 0.62 ≈ 1.58, which is impossible: actual discharge can never exceed ideal discharge, so Cd can never exceed 1.
Dropping the velocity of approach in a narrow channel. The formula then uses H + h<sub>a</sub>, with h<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>a</sub>²/2g, not H alone.

quiz.q: Define Cc, Cv and Cd for an orifice, and give the relation between them.
quiz.a: Cc = jet area at the vena contracta / hole area, about 0.62. Cv = actual jet velocity / theoretical velocity √(2gH), about 0.98. Cd = actual discharge / theoretical discharge, and Cd = Cc × Cv, about 0.62.

quiz.q: State the discharge coefficient of an external cylindrical mouthpiece and of a Borda mouthpiece.
quiz.a: External cylindrical mouthpiece: Cd ≈ 0.82. Borda (internal, re-entrant) mouthpiece: Cd ≈ 0.5.

quiz.q: Why does a short external tube on a hole discharge more than the bare hole?
quiz.a: The jet contracts inside the tube instead of in open air. The space between the vena contracta and the outlet runs below atmospheric pressure, and this suction draws extra water through, raising Cd from about 0.62 to about 0.82. The tube must stay full.

quiz.q: A sharp-edged orifice of diameter 50 mm has its centre 2 m below the water surface in a large tank. Take Cd = 0.62. Find the discharge in litres per second.
A 90° V-notch has a head of 0.25 m over its vertex. Take Cd = 0.6. Find the discharge.

A weir spans the full width of a channel. A second identical crest is installed clear of both side walls. At the same head, which one passes less water, and by what fraction? Use one end-contraction term.
quiz.a: The crest clear of both walls has two end contractions, n = 2, so L<sub>eff</sub> = L − 0.2H, while the suppressed crest has L<sub>eff</sub> = L. Since Q is proportional to effective length, the contracting crest passes less water by the fraction 0.2H/L, for example 2.7 % for H = 0.4 m and L = 3 m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Field installations rarely trust a bare sharp-crested weir for accurate measurement: the crest rusts, weeds catch on it, and the coefficient drifts from its table value. Long-throated flumes and the Parshall flume hold a stable coefficient over a wide range and lose much less head, so irrigation canals and sewage plants prefer them. A V-notch weir survives where the flow is small and the water clean, such as a laboratory channel or a hillside spring. Modern practice calibrates the structure in place with a current meter or an ultrasonic level gauge rather than relying on a coefficient. Search for "long-throated flume" or "Sutro weir" to see shapes whose discharge is made nearly linear in head.
